summary: Describes how SCTP maps into the sockets programming interface. It aims for compatibility with TCP applications while providing access to SCTP features and a unified way to handle events and errors. This is an informational document for programmers.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6458 explains how programs use SCTP through the familiar sockets API. It defines one style for a socket that handles many associations and another that handles one association like a TCP socket.

subtitle: How applications use SCTP through one-to-many or one-to-one sockets.

tldr.problem: SCTP combines message-based data transfer with connection-oriented associations and features such as multiple streams and addresses. The standard sockets calls need a defined mapping to support both familiar programming styles and SCTP-specific controls.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6458 defines one-to-many sockets with SOCK_SEQPACKET and one-to-one sockets with SOCK_STREAM, plus ancillary data, notifications, socket options, and SCTP-specific functions.
tldr.outcome: The document describes an Informational sockets API mapping. It aims to ease migration from TCP applications while providing access to SCTP features.

today: RFC 6458 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata. It describes the SCTP sockets API as published in December 2011.

sections.title: Mapping SCTP to Sockets
sections.content:
The sockets API gives applications a common way to access Internet protocols. SCTP has characteristics of TCP and message-oriented behavior more like UDP, so RFC 6458 defines a sockets mapping that supports both TCP-like and one-to-many programming styles.

The mapping uses common socket data types where possible. SCTP applications create sockets using the SCTP protocol identifier and choose a socket style through the socket type. New SCTP functions cover operations that existing socket calls cannot express adequately.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC explains how an application can call SCTP through the familiar sockets interface. It defines two socket styles because SCTP does not fit only one existing programming pattern.

sections.title: The Two Socket Styles
sections.content:
In the one-to-many style, one SOCK_SEQPACKET socket can represent multiple SCTP associations. Each association has an identifier, and a server receives new associations automatically rather than calling accept(). Applications use message calls such as sendmsg() and recvmsg() to exchange data.

In the one-to-one style, a SOCK_STREAM socket controls one association, similar to a TCP socket. A server listens and uses accept() to obtain a new socket descriptor for each association; a client initiates an association with connect().

An application can separate one association from a one-to-many socket with sctp_peeloff(), which returns a socket for that association. SCTP does not support TCP-style half-close behavior, so programs using shutdown() may need changes when ported.
sections.plainLanguage: One socket style handles several associations and identifies each one separately. The other gives each association its own socket and follows the familiar connect-and-accept pattern.

sections.title: Binding, Sending, and Closing
sections.content:
An SCTP endpoint can use multiple local transport addresses but one local port. The standard bind() call is used once; sctp_bindx() adds support for associating multiple addresses. If an application does not bind before starting an association, the system can select an ephemeral port and address set.

Sending data to a peer without an existing association can cause SCTP to establish one implicitly. The API also supports explicit connection setup. A one-to-many socket's close() gracefully shuts down its associations; an individual association can be gracefully ended with SCTP_EOF or aborted with SCTP_ABORT.

SCTP flow control can make a shared one-to-many send buffer a concern: one stalled association may block sends on other associations if they share buffer space. The RFC discusses separate association buffers, non-blocking operation, or one-to-one sockets as ways to avoid this problem.
sections.plainLanguage: An endpoint can use several network addresses while keeping one local port. On a shared socket, a stalled association can affect other associations if they share the same send buffer.

sections.title: Per-Message Information and Notifications
sections.content:
The msghdr structure lets an application send and receive SCTP-specific ancillary data alongside a user message. When sending, that data can select behavior such as the stream to use; when receiving, it can describe the message. The RFC separates newer send and receive information structures from the older combined structure, which is marked deprecated.

Applications can also receive notifications through recvmsg(). Notifications report events such as association changes, peer-address changes, shutdown, and send failures. The application enables the notification types it wants through SCTP socket options, and must size its control buffer to receive the ancillary data it needs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message can carry extra control information, such as which SCTP stream to use. The SCTP stack can also deliver notifications about changes to an association or its peer addresses.

sections.title: Socket Options and SCTP Functions
sections.content:
Socket options let an application read or change SCTP settings. The RFC describes controls for retransmission timeouts, association initialization, delayed acknowledgments, fragmentation, primary addresses, authentication, and association status. Some options are deprecated because newer options replaced them.

Additional functions support operations such as binding or connecting multiple addresses, retrieving address lists, and separating an association from a shared socket. The document specifies the arguments and behavior for each function so applications and implementations can interoperate.
sections.plainLanguage: Socket options expose SCTP settings such as timeouts and address preferences. Additional SCTP functions support address lists and association management that ordinary socket calls do not cover.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC recommends restricting binding to port numbers below 1024 to privileged users on platforms that use that distinction. It also warns against allowing unprivileged users to choose parameters that make congestion control more aggressive than allowed on the public Internet.

One-to-many sockets with fragment interleave level zero can be exposed to denial-of-service behavior described by the RFC. Applications that need transport-layer security can use DTLS/SCTP as specified in RFC 6083.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations should restrict access to low-numbered ports and prevent users from configuring overly aggressive congestion behavior. Applications can use DTLS/SCTP when they need transport-layer security.
